messages.subject: Re: What is the C matrix?
parts:
Hi Soroush,

Thanks for your interest in Canopy. I updated answer to your question on our GitHub page: https://github.com/yuchaojiang/Canopy (see common questions). Basically, if you don’t have overlapping CNAs, you can leave the C matrix as null. If you do have overlapping CNAs however, we recommend manual inspection and visualization of the overlapped events (because given a region, we don’t know from the observed sequencing data how many CNA events there are unless we see different change in copy number or different breakpoint in the same region). The rows of the C matrix are CNA REGIONS and the columns of the C matrix are CNA EVENTS.

Let me know if this clarifies,

Cheers,
Yuchao

On Sep 28, 2016, at 11:23 AM, Soroush Samadian <Soroush....@uhnresearch.ca> wrote:

Hi Yuchao,

This is Soroush; I am a post-doc fellow at Princess Margaret Cancer. I've been working on tumor clonal evolution on different projects (I have used PhyloWGS, PyClone, Clomial, TITAN and more in the past) and I've found Canopy really interesting. I only have one quick question.

At conceptual level I am still not sure I understand the "C" matrix and how I can create it from my own data(e.g. from Sequenza output). For instance the C matrix in your toy example looks like the following:


          chr7_1  chr7_2  chr12_1   chr12_2  chr18  chr19
chr7       1         1           0          0             0         0
chr12      0        0           1          1             0         0
chr18      0        0           0          0             1         0
chr19      0        0           0          0             0         1


I am still not quite sure what's meant by that and/or how I can create it from my own data. In the example it says:

"      whether CNA regions harbor specific CNAs (only needed for overlapping CNAs)    "



I'd appreciate if you could elaborate on this.

Thanks in advance,

Soroush
